headline: High: shared filesystem and MCP/Claude-Code surfaces create default prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict risks between agentic-flow and ctx.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, and agent_b reads filesystem plus observes Claude Code events; that creates a plausible content-bridging path where one agent’s outputs can be treated as instructions by the other. The pair lacks documented provenance isolation, so the interaction exists in default-ish setups, though not as directly as a raw shared queue.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled text into a file or MCP message that agent_b later parses as instructions
IF agent_b consumes Claude Code event content or workspace files without provenance filtering
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to every cross-agent artifact
Restrict agent_b to read-only parsing of agent_a outputs
Place agent_a and agent_b in separate workspaces
Disable MCP ingestion for untrusted content
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches repository metadata, task prompts, and code, while agent_b touches audit/runtime logs, harness records, and filesystem data. Because agent_b has filesystem access and both expose API surfaces, shared-workspace leakage is plausible in default configurations even without explicit secret-handling overlap. The evidence is indirect, so I choose medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same workspace directory
IF agent_b reads files produced by agent_a that contain prompts, repository metadata, or logs
mitigations: Use separate per-agent directories
Mount sensitive inputs read-only
Redact prompts before writing shared artifacts
Limit log retention to minimal fields
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell commands, modify git state, install packages, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b can install packages and run browsers, and both support multiple instances. In a shared repo or workspace, concurrent writes and package changes can race and corrupt state. Because the profiles do not show locking, the dangerous default is high.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a writable repository or dependency environment
IF either agent modifies git state or installs packages while the other is active
mitigations: Serialize writes with a lock file
Use separate virtual environments
Pin dependencies before concurrent runs
Pause one agent during git operations
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutual exclusion

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_b observes Claude Code events and agent_a emits outputs through MCP/stdin-stdout, so agent_b can treat agent_a’s output as authoritative unless an explicit verification step exists. That creates a realistic cascade from one agent’s mistaken output into the other’s downstream actions, but the profiles do not show direct autonomous external actions, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output as ground truth without validation
IF agent_b uses observed events to trigger follow-on actions based on agent_a-produced content
mitigations: Require a verification step before acting on agent_a output
Mark agent_a outputs as untrusted by default
Log source provenance alongside derived actions
Add human review for high-impact actions
requires-engineering: implement confidence-gated action routing

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. agent_a handles task prompts and repository metadata, while agent_b handles audit/runtime logs and harness records; that suggests a possible policy mismatch if combined, but the profiles do not prove a regulated-data pathway. I therefore keep this low and cite both profiles because the risk depends on their differing data classes.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into agent_a prompts or agent_b logs
IF the deployment requires a retention or residency policy that differs between the two agents
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent
Set a shared retention policy
Avoid placing regulated data in prompts
Review vendor/data-processing terms
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across both agents
